notes.meaning: The famine in Canaan did not end quickly, but grew heavier as time passed. Jacob and his family lived in the promised land, yet they still faced deep hardship and hunger. God allowed this shortage so that Jacob's family would have to turn to Egypt, where Joseph was waiting.

The grain the brothers brought from their first trip was now completely eaten. Jacob told his sons to travel back to Egypt and buy a small amount of food to keep the household alive. He asked for just a little because food was scarce and times were hard.

Judah spoke up and reminded his father that the Egyptian ruler had laid down a strict condition. The ruler warned them with a solemn oath that they could never appear before him again without Benjamin. Judah made it clear that traveling without their youngest brother would be useless and dangerous, so they would only go if Benjamin went with them.

Jacob was heartbroken and blamed his sons for causing him more grief. He asked why they had ever mentioned having another brother to the Egyptian ruler. From Jacob's viewpoint, sharing that detail seemed like an unnecessary mistake that put his favorite child in danger.

The brothers explained that the ruler had questioned them closely about their family and background. Because he accused them of being spies, they had to answer honestly to clear their names. They pointed out that they had no way of knowing he would demand to see Benjamin.

Judah urged his father to entrust Benjamin to him so they could leave immediately. He reminded Jacob that if they stayed home, everyone in the family—including the children and Benjamin himself—would starve to death. Going to Egypt was their only hope for survival.

Judah took full personal responsibility for Benjamin's safety. He promised that if he failed to bring Benjamin back alive, he would carry the blame and guilt before his father for the rest of his life. This showed real change in Judah, who had once led the effort to sell Joseph into slavery.
Judah pointed out that Jacob's hesitation had only prolonged their hunger and wasted valuable time. If they had not delayed in Canaan, they could have completed two round trips to Egypt by now.

Jacob finally gave in to what could not be avoided, but he took careful steps to make peace with the Egyptian ruler. He told his sons to pack gifts of Canaan’s finest local products, including balm, honey, spices, myrrh, pistachios, and almonds. Even during a famine, these luxury goods were still available and could help soften the ruler's heart.

Jacob told his sons to take double the silver with them. This was to pay for new grain and to return the silver they had found in their sacks from the first trip. Jacob treated the returned silver as an honest mistake, showing fairness and integrity in his dealings.
With all the preparations made, Jacob told his sons to take Benjamin and set out for Egypt right away. He knew he had to let go of his beloved son if the family was going to survive.

Jacob prayed that God Almighty would give his sons mercy before the Egyptian ruler, so that both Simeon and Benjamin would return safely. He placed his family into God's hands, quietly submitting to whatever God allowed to happen, even if it meant losing his children.

differ.view: Jacob's words show genuine faith and humble submission to God's providence rather than fatalism.
Jacob's words show real faith mixed with fatalism and fear.

notes.meaning: The brothers gathered the gifts, the double silver, and Benjamin, and hurried down to Egypt. When they arrived, they presented themselves before Joseph at the place where he managed the grain sales.

When Joseph saw Benjamin among them, he told the steward of his house to take the men home and prepare a midday feast. He was eager to welcome them, but he still had public business to finish before he could sit down to eat.
The steward followed Joseph's instructions and brought the brothers to Joseph’s private residence.

Being taken to the governor's mansion terrified the brothers instead of comforting them. Their guilty consciences made them fear the worst, imagining they were being lured inside so the ruler could seize them as slaves and steal their donkeys over the returned silver.

The brothers stopped the steward at the front door before going inside, eager to clear their names right away. They explained politely that their only goal on their first trip was simply to buy food for their family.

They told the steward that when they opened their sacks during their journey home, each man found his full payment placed in the mouth of his sack. They explained that they had brought that money back along with extra silver to buy more grain, insisting they had no idea who put the silver there.

The steward calmed their fears, telling them that their money had safely reached his hands and that their father's God had given them treasure in their sacks. Joseph had apparently taught his household about the true God of the Hebrews. To reassure them even further, the steward brought Simeon out to rejoin them.
The steward welcomed the men into the house and showed them warm hospitality. He provided water to wash the dust from their feet and gave food to their donkeys.
Learning that they would be eating lunch with the governor, the brothers laid out their gifts to present to Joseph when he arrived at noon.

When Joseph arrived, the brothers presented their gifts and bowed down to the earth before him. This act of deep respect was another fulfillment of the dreams God had given Joseph years earlier, showing his brothers bowing before him.

Joseph warmly asked how they were doing and inquired if their elderly father was still alive and well. The brothers replied respectfully that their father was alive and in good health, bowing down once again to honor Joseph.

Joseph looked at Benjamin, his only full brother born to his mother Rachel, and asked if this was the youngest brother they had mentioned. Before Benjamin could even reply, Joseph blessed him, asking God to be gracious to him.
Overwhelmed with love and deep affection for his brother, Joseph hurried out of the room to find a private place to weep. He went into his personal bedroom and wept freely where no one could see him.
After weeping, Joseph washed his face to hide his tears, regained his composure, and returned to the room. He then commanded his servants to serve the meal.

The servants set three separate tables: one for Joseph, one for his brothers, and one for the Egyptian guests. The Egyptians held strict cultural and religious rules that treated eating with Hebrews as detestable, while Joseph's high rank also set him apart.

Joseph had his brothers seated across from him in exact order of their ages, from the oldest to the youngest. The brothers looked at one another in total amazement, wondering how an Egyptian ruler could know their birth order so perfectly.

Joseph sent food to them from his own table, giving Benjamin five times as much as any of the others to honor him and test if the older brothers still harbored jealousy. With their fears put to rest, the brothers relaxed and enjoyed a joyful feast with Joseph.
